strengths: Extensive empirical validation spanning model architectures (dense LLaMA, MoE Qwen2MoE), scales (66M–2B), datasets (C4, OpenWebText), and LR schedules (cosine, wsd), with consistent and reproducible gains for AdamWPower over well-tuned AdamW baselines.
Demonstrates scaling-law benefits (FLOP savings) rather than only fixed-scale improvements, which is more convincing evidence of practical utility at larger scales.
Shows compatibility/orthogonality with other state-of-the-art optimizer improvements (Muon, Blockwise LR), suggesting the method is a genuinely modular plug-in rather than a substitute.

Careful ablations: order of clipping vs. GradPower, robustness to (β1, β2) tuning, multi-seed variance analysis, downstream zero-shot benchmark evaluation, and wall-clock overhead measurement (~0.4%), which strengthen practical credibility.

Provides a plausible theoretical account (toy 1D model plus formal AdaGrad convergence theorems in low-/high-noise regimes) that qualitatively matches the empirically observed dependence of the optimal power p on batch size/noise level.
Transparent about the extremely close relationship to the pre-existing Powerball method, disclosed in an appendix, which is commendable scholarly honesty even though it affects perceived novelty.
The method truly is a one-line, hyperparameter-free (given single p) change to existing pipelines, which is appealing for practical adoption.
weaknesses: Core technical novelty is limited: the sign-power gradient transform is essentially the pre-existing Powerball method (Yuan et al., 2019), and the paper's own appendix acknowledges this was discovered only after completing the work; the main contribution is thus largely the empirical/theoretical extension to modern LLM optimizers rather than a new algorithmic idea.

Theoretical convergence guarantees are derived for AdaGrad, not for Adam/AdamW (the actual method evaluated at scale); the gap between the analyzed algorithm and the deployed algorithm (which includes momentum, bias correction, weight decay) leaves the formal link between theory and the main empirical method incomplete.

The illustrative case study (Example 5.1) relies on a highly simplified 1D uniform-noise, single-step-limit setting; while illustrative, its predictive power for high-dimensional, non-stationary LLM training dynamics is only qualitatively/anecdotally validated.

The power p is tuned on a single small-scale configuration (LLaMA 0.2B on C4) and then reused as p=1.2 across essentially all other settings; while the paper argues this generalizes well, the tuning protocol is thin and could risk being specific to the particular architecture/data regime tested, despite claims of robustness.

Explanations for some of the more striking empirical phenomena (e.g., improved training stability and outsized benefit for MoE models) remain speculative ('we hypothesize…leave to future work'), which weakens the mechanistic understanding of why the method is particularly effective in these settings.

Absolute loss improvements in many plots (e.g., Figure 3, Figure 4) are numerically small, and the paper does not report confidence intervals/statistical significance uniformly across all main results (only a subset in Appendix B.4), making it harder to fully assess whether gains are consistently significant versus run-to-run noise at larger scales.
Comparisons with other advanced optimizers/preconditioners (e.g., Shampoo, Sophia, Adam-mini) are absent; the compatibility study is limited to only Muon and Blockwise LR.
